passages.original: Tantumne opinionis adsumpsisse homines, ut aliqui eorum tria principia constituerent omnium, deum et exemplar et materiam, sicut Plato discipulique eius, et ea incorrupta et increata ac sine initio esse adseuerarent deumque non tamquam creatorem materiae, sed tamquam artificem ad exemplar, hoc est ideam intendentem fecisse mundum de materia, quam uocant ὕλην, quae gignendi causas rebus omnibus dedisse adseratur, ipsum quoque mundum incorruptum nec creatum aut factum aestimarent, alii quoque, ut Aristoteles cum suis disputandum putauit, duo principia ponerent, materiam et speciem, et tertium cum his, quod operatorium dicitur, cui subpeteret competenter efficere quod adoriendum putasset.
passages.english: That men should have taken up so much [false] opinion that some of them established three first principles of all things, god, the exemplar, and matter, as Plato and his disciples [did], and asserted that these are incorruptible and uncreated and without beginning; and [held] that god made the world not as the creator of matter but as a craftsman directing his attention to an exemplar, that is, an idea, [making it] out of matter, which they call *hylē* [matter], which is asserted to have given the causes of generation to all things; and that they reckoned the world itself also to be incorruptible and neither created nor made; [and that] others too, as Aristotle with his followers thought should be argued, posited two first principles, matter and form, and with these a third, which is called the operative [principle], to which it belonged to accomplish fittingly whatever it thought should be undertaken!
passages.notes: The sentence is an exclamatory accusative-and-infinitive construction expressing indignation; its main clause is implied. 'Opinionis' here implies mere or false opinion.

passages.original: nam Pythagoras unum mundum adserit, alii innumerabiles dicunt esse mundos, ut scribit Democritus, cui plurimum de physicis auctoritatis uetustas detulit, ipsumque mundum semper fuisse et fore Aristoteles usurpat dicere: contra autem Plato non semper fuisse et semper fore praesumit adstruere, plurimi uero non fuisse semper nec semper fore scriptis suis testificantur.
passages.english: For Pythagoras asserts that there is one world; others say that there are innumerable worlds, as Democritus writes, to whom antiquity has granted the greatest authority on natural philosophy; and Aristotle takes it upon himself to say that the world itself always was and always will be; Plato, on the other hand, presumes to maintain that it did not always exist but will always exist; while very many testify in their writings that it neither always existed nor will always exist.

passages.original: Moyses utique ille eruditus in omni sapientia Aegyptiorum, quem de flumine collectum filia Pharao ut filium dilexit et subsidiis regalibus tultumfultum omnibus saecularis prudentiae disciplinis informari atque instrui desiderauit. qui cum de aqua nomen acceperit, non putauit tamen dicendum quod ex aqua constarent omnia, ut Thales dicit, et cum esset in aula educatus regia, maluit tamen pro amore iustitiae subire exilium uoluntarium quam in tyrannidis fastigio peccati perfunctionem deliciis adquirere. denique priusquam ad populi liberandi munus uocaretur, naturali aequitatis studio prouocatus accipientem iniuriam de popularibus suis ultus inuidiae sese dedit uoluptatique eripuit atque omnis regiae domus declinans tumultus in secretum Aethiopiae se contulit ibique a ceteris negotiis remotus totum diuinae cognitioni animum intendit, ut gloriam dei uideret faciem ad faciem. cui testificatur scriptura quia nemo surrexit amplius propheta in Istrahel sicut Moyses, qui sciuit dominum faciem ad faciem, non in uisione neque in somnio, sed os ad os cum deo summo locutus, neque in specie neque per aenigmata, sed clara atque perspicua praesentiae diuinae dignatione donatus.
passages.english: Moses, certainly, that man learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, whom, taken up from the river, Pharaoh's daughter loved as a son, and whom, supported by royal resources, she wished to be formed and instructed in all the disciplines of worldly wisdom. Although he received his name from water, he nevertheless did not think it should be said that all things consist of water, as Thales says; and although he was brought up in the royal court, he nevertheless preferred, for love of justice, to undergo voluntary exile rather than to acquire, at the summit of tyranny, the enjoyment of sin through pleasures. Then, before he was called to the task of freeing the people, roused by a natural zeal for equity, he avenged one of his countrymen who was suffering injury, exposed himself to ill will and tore himself away from pleasure, and, avoiding all the turmoil of the royal house, withdrew to the seclusion of Ethiopia; and there, removed from other affairs, he directed his whole mind to the knowledge of God, so as to see the glory of God face to face. To him Scripture bears witness that no prophet has arisen again in Israel like Moses, who knew the Lord face to face, not in a vision or in a dream, but speaking mouth to mouth with the most high God, neither in appearance nor through riddles, but endowed with the clear and evident favour of the divine presence.
passages.notes: 'tultumfultum' is a scanning doublet; read 'fultum' (supported). 'peccati perfunctionem' is rendered 'enjoyment of sin'; the sense of 'perfunctio' is somewhat uncertain. The first sentence lacks a main verb in the transmitted text, presumably continuing a thought from the preceding context.
